challenges.name: saturation-knee-table
challenges.title: Read the knee from a step table
challenges.description: Two statements on the step load test of one API instance: what happens to extra load past the knee, and which signal shows the knee first.

questions.question:
Step load test of POST /api/submissions on ONE API instance (pool of 6 DB connections), 2 minutes per step, warm-up excluded:

offered/s  achieved/s  p95       errors
   100       100.0      66 ms    0.00%
   110       110.0      70 ms    0.00%
   120       119.9      79 ms    0.00%
   130       129.9     104 ms    0.00%
   140       139.8     205 ms    0.00%
   150       149.1     820 ms    0.00%
   160       157.2     3.9 s     0.00%
   170       157.9     8.4 s     0.20%
   180       158.1    12.1 s     2.60%

Statement: "From 160/s on, the extra offered load is not served at all: achieved throughput stays at about 158/s, so every additional request per second only adds to a waiting line, and p95 grows with it."
questions.explanation: True. The instance's ceiling is about 158 requests per second (6 connections / 38 ms hold time). Above it, achieved throughput stops following offered load, and the difference - about 3 requests per second at 160, 12 at 170, 22 at 180 - joins a queue that grows for the whole step, which is why p95 climbs from seconds to more than 12 s and why timeouts appear at the end. The misconception is that higher load gives proportionally more throughput with somewhat slower responses; past the ceiling it gives no more throughput and much slower responses.

questions.question:
Step load test of POST /api/submissions on ONE API instance (pool of 6 DB connections), 2 minutes per step, warm-up excluded:

offered/s  achieved/s  p95       errors
   100       100.0      66 ms    0.00%
   110       110.0      70 ms    0.00%
   120       119.9      79 ms    0.00%
   130       129.9     104 ms    0.00%
   140       139.8     205 ms    0.00%
   150       149.1     820 ms    0.00%
   160       157.2     3.9 s     0.00%
   170       157.9     8.4 s     0.20%
   180       158.1    12.1 s     2.60%

Statement: "The knee of this instance is at 170/s, because 170/s is the first step where achieved throughput falls below 95% of the offered rate."
questions.explanation: False. Throughput is the last signal to move: it only drops below the offered rate once the queue grows without limit. Latency moves first. The p95 more than doubles from the low-load 66 ms by 140/s (205 ms) and reaches 820 ms at 150/s, while throughput still keeps up. With the course's rule (the last step before the first step that breaks any of throughput, latency or errors), the knee is 130/s. Planning capacity at 170/s would put learners in front of a multi-second queue. The misconception is to read the knee from the throughput curve alone.

challenges.name: find-the-saturation-knee
challenges.title: Find the saturation knee in a step test
challenges.description:
Before every exam, CodeDev runs a step load test of POST /api/submissions on one API instance and records one row per step. The capacity plan uses the knee: the highest offered rate at which the instance still behaves like it does at low load. Write find_knee(case) with exactly this rule, so that every engineer reads the same table the same way.

Input (stdin, JSON): {"min_throughput_ratio": R, "max_p95_factor": F, "max_error_rate": E, "steps": [{"offered_rps", "achieved_rps", "p95_ms", "requests", "errors"}, ...]}. offered_rps is the rate the load generator tried to send, achieved_rps the responses per second it got (any status), p95_ms the p95 latency of the step (computed by the load tool with the course's nearest-rank definition: rank = ceil(p/100 * n), value = sorted[rank - 1]), requests the requests sent in the step and errors how many of them failed. Steps can be in any order. Valid rows have distinct offered rates.

Rule:
1. A row is valid when it is an object whose five fields are all numbers (int or float, not bool) with offered_rps > 0, requests > 0, achieved_rps >= 0, p95_ms > 0 and 0 <= errors <= requests. Ignore every other row and count it in "ignored_rows".
2. Sort the valid rows by offered_rps. The baseline is the p95_ms of the lowest row.
3. A row breaks a rule when:
   - "throughput": achieved_rps / offered_rps < R (the system no longer keeps up),
   - "latency": p95_ms > F * baseline (latency left the low-load level),
   - "errors": errors / requests > E.
   Values exactly on a threshold do not break it.
4. The first row (lowest offered_rps) that breaks at least one rule is the first saturated step. The knee is the offered_rps of the valid row just before it, or null when the lowest row already breaks a rule. A later row that looks healthy again does not move the knee.
5. If no row breaks a rule, the knee was not reached in the tested range: knee_rps is the highest offered_rps tested and reached is false.

Output: {"knee_rps": number or null, "first_saturated_rps": number or null, "reasons": the broken rules of the first saturated step in the order throughput, latency, errors ([] if none), "baseline_p95_ms": number or null, "reached": true if a step broke a rule, "ignored_rows": count}. With no valid row: knee_rps, first_saturated_rps and baseline_p95_ms are null, reasons [], reached false.

Example: steps 100, 110, 120, 130, 140 with p95 66, 70, 79, 104, 205 ms, throughput keeping up and no errors, R = 0.95, F = 2.0, E = 0.01 -> {"knee_rps": 130, "first_saturated_rps": 140, "reasons": ["latency"], "baseline_p95_ms": 66, "reached": true, "ignored_rows": 0}.
hints: Which of the three signals - throughput, latency, errors - would you expect to move first as a pool or queue fills up, and which last? Does your function look at all three for every row?

Check the order of operations: drop invalid rows before you sort and before you pick the baseline (the baseline is the lowest valid row, not the first row of the input). Then walk the sorted rows once and stop at the first row with any broken rule; compare with strict < and > so that values exactly on a threshold pass.

A worked example on other data: offered 20, 40, 60, 80 req/s; achieved 20, 40, 57, 61; p95 30, 32, 41, 300 ms; no errors; R = 0.95, F = 2.0. Baseline 30 ms, so latency breaks above 60 ms. At 60: 57 / 60 = 0.95 is not below 0.95 and 41 ms is not above 60 ms, so it is healthy. At 80: 61 / 80 = 0.76 breaks throughput and 300 ms breaks latency, so the first saturated step is 80 with reasons throughput, latency, and the knee is 60.

tests.name: Per-instance submit step test: latency doubles before throughput stops tracking
Errors are the first signal: fast 503s keep latency and throughput looking fine
Throughput falls first, with errors at the same step: both reasons in order
Values exactly on a threshold are still healthy
Unsorted steps and a step that recovers: the knee is before the first bad step
The lowest step already fails: no knee in the tested range
Invalid rows are ignored; a table that never saturates did not reach the knee
Large input: 400 steps of 1 req/s, shuffled
